en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Homage to the Introduction for Beginners.
[Ka] He has reached the further shore of the entire path of linguistic expression;
he is the Awakened One, the ornament of the three worlds, who has destroyed all unwholesome states.
Having constantly paid homage to the Dhamma,
which bestows the bliss of liberation and destroys the mass of evil, and to the Saṅgha, who are worthy of offerings;
[Kha]
I am grown old and foolish, yet my supreme reverence for the Buddha— resplendent with virtue,

wisdom, and other virtues— is undiminished. I bow my head in constant salutation, remembering him who has passed away, relying upon the pure radiance of the sublime Conqueror’s Teaching, which shines like the sun and moon.
[Ga] By the power of her lotus-feet, which are the pinnacle of virtue and have destroyed the stain of evil,
[he composed] the ancient Sinhala word-commentary and its analysis.
Having properly reflected upon the entire system of Magadhi grammar as it has been praised,
as well as the many other various types of respected grammatical treatises and the doctrines handed down through tradition.
[Gha] This *Bālāvatāra* is the best among the Magadha grammatical treatises,
owing to its determination of the meanings of many words that are difficult to understand.
For the benefit of the modern succession of the ignorant,
I shall compose this *Bālāvatāra*, a selection of excellent glosses on difficult points. [Ṅa]
May those fools here who are always endowed with noble hearts and have well-fixed their eyes,
being full of various methods like a celestial tree and worthy of the wise’s praise—
may they possess the strength to cross the deep and difficult-to-traverse ocean of the Conqueror’s word.
And those who, having obtained the means, desire to hear the Moon and its other abundant, honored [commentaries],
[should understand] the difficulty of producing the text as it truly is; for the remainder— [the task of] completing the work— is arduous.
The wise and skilled understand the merits and faults in books, such as various treatises and so forth;
they alone are always the ones who possess true discernment. [6]
Therefore, if there should be even a trace of fault here, such as negligence or the like,
or if it should contradict the views attained by the ancient masters, [then let it be so]. [Ja]
"Having plunged into other texts and investigated them again and again,
let those who possess investigative intelligence grasp only what is logically consistent.
Homage.
1. Having paid homage three times to the Buddha, whose eyes are like lotuses, I shall expound the *Bālāvatāra* for the increase of the intelligence of beginners. 1.
The Section on Phonetics (*Sandhikaṇḍa*).
Perception 2.
There are forty-one syllables and words.
The syllables, beginning with *a*, are also forty-one and are helpful for the Suttantas. They are as follows: *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o; ka, kha*.
ga gha ṅa, ca cha ja jha ña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma, ya ra la va sa ha ḷa aṃ.
3. Among these, the vowels ending in "u" are eight.
In that regard, among the syllables (*akkhara*), the eight vowels ending in *o* are called "long" (*sara*).

The word "therein" (*tattha*) is understood to carry over. 4. Three are short by measure of lightness (*lahu-matta*). Among those vowels, *a*, *i*, and *u* are the three short ones by measure of lightness.
5. Others are long.
In that regard, among the short vowels, others are long when following a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).

Short *e* and *o* occurring before a consonant cluster are called long; a consonant cluster consists of consonants occurring without an intervening vowel. Examples here are: *seyyo*, *oṭṭho*, *sotthi*.
6. The remaining are consonants (*byañjana*).
With the vowels set aside, the remaining letters from *ka* to *ma*, ending with the *niggahīta*, are consonants.
7. The classes (*vaggā*) consist of five each.
The consonants, beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, are grouped into five sets of five letters each.

8. Of these sets (*vaggā*), the first and second [consonants] are voiced (*saghosa*). The others, ending in *ḷ*, are unvoiced (*aghosa*). The designations "voiced" and "unvoiced" are included under the rule:
"Technical terms used by others are also employed in this work. Thus: gender, pronouns, nouns, prefixes, particles, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), verbs, and...
And there is the technical designation "kammappavacanīya" and so forth. 9.
*Aṃ* is the *niggahīta*. That nasal dot (*bindu*) which follows the letter *a* is called *niggahīta*.

The *bindu* (anusvāra), having the form of a crest-jewel (*cūḷāmaṇi*), is called the *niggahīta*. Because it is employed independently, the letter *a* is supplied [to it]. 10. *A* is born from the throat; the *ka*-group is born from the palate; *i* is born from the teeth;

the *ca*-group is born from the palate; *yā* is born from the palate; *u* is born from the lips; the *pa*-group is born from the lips; *o* is born from the lips; the *ṭa*-group is born from the head; *ra* and *ḷa* are born from the head; the *ta*-group is born from the teeth; *la* is born from the teeth; *sā* is born from the teeth; *e* is born from the throat and palate; *o* is born from the throat and lips; *vo* is born from the teeth and lips.
Saññā-sarasandhi 11.
Regarding the phrase *loka-aggo*: in the rule "one should separate the preceding consonant from the vowel," the preceding consonant must be separated from the vowel.
Vowels undergo elision before a vowel.
When a following vowel is immediately adjacent, preceding vowels undergo elision.

According to the rule "In the presence of *nara*, the following [vowel] should be joined," a consonant that lacks a vowel must be brought forward to the subsequent letter at the beginning of the word in common usage.

In this [rule], the seventh case (locative) ending is elided when there is proximity (*opasilesika*). Consequently, no grammatical operation occurs when there is an intervention by a vowel (*vaṇṇa*) or a consonant (*kāla*). For example: *maṃ ahā sī* (in the verse beginning with *pamādamanuyuñjanti*), and in the phrase *janā appamādaṃ* from the same verse.

This applies to all sandhi rules. Immediately following, [the author] will state the elision of a subsequent vowel; therefore, by that [subsequent rule], the elision of the preceding [vowel] is understood. By that very fact, the posteriority of what is indicated by the seventh case is also understood. 12. The governing rule (*adhikāra*) for "in a vowel" (*sare*) continues.
However, in the cases of *pana ime* and *pana imete*, the vowels are elided simply by the word *itva*.
Or, a dissimilar [vowel] following [a vowel] may be elided. A vowel following another vowel that is not of the same form may optionally be dropped: *paname*, *panime*.
13. *Bandhussa iva, na upeti itīdha*—here [the rule applies].

In some cases, when a vowel is elided, the non-homogeneous vowel (*asavaṇṇa*) [of the preceding sound] occurs in place of the following vowel that has been elided; thus, for *i*, *u*, and *ic*, the nearest substitutes are *e* and *o*. This applies only to the word *bandhu*. It does not apply to *nopeti*.
14. In this regard: *ayaṃ*, *yāni idha*, *bahu upakāraṃ*, *saddhā idha*, *tathā upamaṃ etasmiṃ*.
Long vowel.

When a preceding vowel is elided, the following vowel sometimes becomes long by way of position (*ṭhānāsanna*). For example: *tatrāyaṃ*, *yānīdha*, *bahūpakāraṃ*, *saddhīdha*, *tathūpamaṃ*. Regarding the phrase *kiṃsu idha*: [the *u* is elided, and the following *i* becomes long].
And *pubba*.
In some cases, when *s* is elided, the preceding *u* becomes long. For example: *kiṃ sūdha*.
(16) *te ajja*, *te ahaṃte'ttha*.
The substitution of *ya* for the final *e*.
When a vowel follows, the final *e* is sometimes replaced by *ya*; here, [in the case of] "tyajja," it is sometimes long when followed by a consonant, as in "tyāhaṃ.
Why "sometimes"? [As in] "nettha."
17. Thus, regarding "anu etītyettha" (in the phrase *anu etīti*):
when a vowel follows, the letter *v* is sometimes substituted for the final *k* or *r* of words ending in *vam*, *ud*, or *an*. As in: *svassa anveti*.
What is the meaning of "kvaci"? It is: "tayassu, sametāyasmā.
18. "Idha ahaṃ tīdha"—the doubling of the *dh* occurs here as well.

In some cases, two [instances] of *dh* occur after *sare* (vowels) and *pare* (consonants). Regarding *dīgha* (long vowels): *idāhaṃ*. Why "in some cases"? [As in: *idheva*. By means of the letter *ca*, it also applies to consonants:
*idha bhikkhave*. 19. *pati* [is used] before *antuṃ*; there is a grammatical operation (*vutti*) here: the *ivaṇṇa* (the vowel *i*) optionally becomes *yaṇ*.

The letter *ya* optionally becomes *sa* after *pa*. When the substitution of *ya* has occurred, by the rule “*sabbaṃ ca ntī*” (all [substitutes] become *nt*), there is in some instances the substitution of *ca*; then, by the rule “*para-dve-bhāvo ṭhāne*,” due to the proximity of the place of articulation (*ṭhānāsanna*) following a vowel (*sara*), there is doubling (*dvitta*) of the subsequent consonant.

Examples: *paccantaṃ*, *vuttiyā*. Why say “optionally”? [Consider: *paṭaggi*. Here, by the rule “*kvaci paṭi patisse*,” *pati* becomes *paṭi*. The inclusion of the term “letter” (*vaṇṇa*) is for the purpose of including both short and long vowels everywhere.
20. *Yathā eveti iha*:
In this context, the *eva* following *yathā* becomes short;
the *e*-vowel of the subsequent word *eva*, etc., optionally becomes *ri*. The preceding [vowel] also becomes short, being close to its position. Examples: *yathariva*, *yatheva*.

21. *Na imassa*, *ti-aṅgikaṃ*, *lahu*, *essati*, *attha-atthaṃ*, *ito-āyati*, *tasmā-iha*, *sabbhi-eva*, *cha-abhiññā*, *putha-eva*, *pā-evatīha* or *tveva*—these are the augmentations (*āgamā*) for *ya*, *va*, *ma*, *da*, *na*, *ta*, *ra*, and *ḷ*.
When a vowel follows, the letters beginning with *y* (i.e., *y*, *r*, *l*, *v*) may optionally be augmented; by the letter *c*, *go* is also included. *Na imassa*, *ti-aṅgikaṃ*, *lahumessati*.
*attadatthaṃ*, *itonāyati*, *tasmātiha*, *sabbhireva*, *chaḷabhiññā*, *puthageva*.
[In the case of] the consonant *rassa* followed by another consonant, in some instances it remains short. *Pageva*.
[The word] *vā* [is used] for what purpose? [Examples: *cha abhiññā*, *putha eva*, *pā eva*.
In this context, the rule “*sare kvaci*” means that the original form (*pakati*) of vowels remains; the meaning is that it retains its own vowel-form and does not undergo modification.
22. In the case of *abhi uggato*:
according to the rule “*abbho abhī*,” the word *abhī* becomes *abbho*. Thus: *abbhuggato*.
Sarasandhi and Byañjanasandhi 23. The heading "consonant" (byañjana) continues [from here].
In some cases, there is only *i*. For example: *so bhikkhu, kacci nu tvam, jānema tanti iha*—[in these instances, the *i* is not elided].
There is also elision (lopa) of [a vowel] there.

When a consonant follows, there is sometimes elision of vowels; in that case where [the vowel] has been elided, the letter *a* is inserted (*āgama*) at that position, and by the word "also" (*ca*), the letters *o* and *u* are likewise included. Example: *sabhikkhu kaccino tvaṃ, jānemu taṃ*.
Why "sometimes" (*kvaci*)? Example: *somuni*.
24. *Ugghosa*, *akkhāta*—these two [terms] refer only to the place [of articulation].

In a consonant group (*vagga*), the voiced and unvoiced [consonants] become the third and first [members] respectively in that same group; this is declared as *ugghosa* when the place [of articulation] is broad (*rassa*).

25. *Para sahasraṃ*, *atippakhoto*—in these cases, the augment *o* is inserted according to the rule "the vowel *o* is inserted before a consonant" (*kvaci o byañjane*). Thus: *parosahassaṃ*. And when there is the augment *ā*: *atippagokho*. 26.
*Ava naddhā* and *atyatra*—in these cases, the vowel *o* replaces *ava* according to the rule "the vowel *o* replaces *ava*" (*o avasse*). Thus: *onaddhā*. Why say "in some cases" (*kvaci*)?
[To show that it does not apply elsewhere: *avasussatu*.
Conjunctions of Consonants.
Niggahīta-sandhi 27.
The section on *niggahīta*. Examples: *kiṃ kato*, *saṃ jāto*, *saṃ ṭhito*, *taṃ dhanaṃ*, *taṃ mittaṃ*. Herein—

Or, [the nasal] of *bindu* becomes the final consonant of its respective group when followed by a consonant of that same group. For example: *kiṅkato*, *sañjāto*, *saṇṭhito*, *taṇdhanaṃ*, *taṃmittaṃ*. Why is it said "or"?
[Because there are exceptions, such as: *na taṃ kammaṃ*.
The *vākāra* (the letter *v*) alone is elided. Masculine gender. 28. The section on *vā* (optionality).
Thus, in this context: "He said this," "He spoke this"—[in these cases], when followed by a vowel (*sare*), [the *v* is optionally elided].
In the case of *sare pare*, [the letter] *m* becomes either *d* or *v*. Thus he said this to him.
What does "or" (*vā*) mean? It means "he conquered me.
29. "That indeed," "for that," thus here—
Regarding *e* and *ai*:
when *he* follows, the nasal dot (*bindu*) optionally becomes *ñ*. In the case of doubling—*taññeva*, *tameva*; *tañhi*, *taṃ hi*.
30. Here, "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) refers to—
And *saye*.
When followed by the letter *ya*, the *bindu* (anusvāra) optionally becomes *ñ* together with it. In the case of doubling (*dvitte*)—*saññogo*, *saṃyogo*.
31. *Cakkhu aniccaṃ*, *ava sirotīha*—there is an augment (*āgamo*), in some cases only.
And regarding *niggahīta*:
when followed by a vowel or a consonant, a *bindu* (anusvāra) is sometimes inserted. For example:
*cakkhuṃ aniccaṃ*, *avaṃ siro*. 32. *vidūnaṃ aggaṃ*, *tāsaṃ ahaṃ iha*.
“In some cases there is elision”: when a vowel follows, there is elision of the *bindu* (anusvāra), as in *vidūnaggaṃ*. When a long vowel follows, it is *tāsāhaṃ*.

33. In *buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ*, because *saṃ* means “it adheres here,” there is elision of the *bindu* by the rule “if a consonant follows,” resulting in *buddhānasāsanaṃ*. When a long vowel follows, it is *sārāgo*.
34. "Like a seed" (bījaṃ va) means here:
either the following vowel or the *bindu*.
Either the vowel following the *bindu* is elided, as in the word "seed" (*bījaṃ*).
35. Thus it is here:
"The consonant and its disjunction.
When vowels following a *bindu* are elided, the conjunction of consonants becomes a "lost conjunction" (*vinaṭṭhasaṃyoga*), and thus the preceding vowel is dropped. Hence: *evaṃsa*.
Niggahīta-sandhi.
Miscellaneous Sandhis 36.
[This is] because of the application stated for those not specifically mentioned.

Here, the underlying principles (*sandhayo*) not explicitly stated should be understood according to what has been taught—for example: "If it is thus, [the word] *bojjhaṅga* [is formed]"—whereby, by this rule, there is *ja* for the consonant cluster *daya*, *jha* for the consonant cluster *dhaya*, and doubling (*dvitte*) occurs: "If it is thus, *bojjhaṅgā*. 37.

And there is the single form (*ekasarūpatā*) in the case of an uncommon consonant cluster (*asadisa-saṃyoge*). For example: "In the search (*pari-esanā*)"—whereby, by the rule for *ya*-substitution, there is *ya* for the letter *ra*, resulting in *payyesanā*.
38. Multiplicity of vowels, and also their reversal.
“She remembers” (*sarati*), thus indeed; she is a woman (*itthī*); “chaff” (*busaṃ*) indeed; “much affliction” (*bahu-ābādho*); “he was superior” (*adhi-abhavi*);
“pleasure,” “suffering,” “living here” (*jīvoti iha*).—The addition of *m* occurs before *sakāra*, and the vowel *u* replaces *akāra* [in the case of] “he remembers” (*sumarati*).
*Issa vo*: in the word *ittheva*, the vowel *ā* becomes *o*; thus, *sotthī*.
In *mādese*, the long vowel of the preceding syllable [becomes short], and the vowel *e* becomes *i*; thus, *busāmiva*.
In *vāde*, there is the reversal of *ha* and *ka*. In *bahv-ābādho*, [the vowel] is long.
In *adhissa*, it is sometimes short; in *dīgha-addhābhavi*, [it is long].
For the bindu and for the vowel *o*, [there is] *e*. In *sukhe*, *dukkhe*, and *jīve*.
39. *Ra*, *da*, *naṃ*, *ḷo*, *paṭibodho*, *pariḷāho*. 40.

When *sa* or a consonant follows, the *bindu* (anusvāra) sometimes becomes *mo*. In *mama abhāsi*, *buddhama saraṇaṃ*, and *pubbe mo paraṃ na netabbo*, it should not be changed to *ma* because that would be improper.
41. After a *bindu*, there is also the substitution of *mañña* for *sara*.
"Taṃ iminā, evaṃ imaṃ, kiṃ ahaṃ tīha-issa a. Tadaminā.
Issa u, akārassa ca e, bindulopādo. Evumaṃ, kehaṃ.
(42) For the sake of easy pronunciation in a sentence, and for the purpose of avoiding metrical loss, there is also the elision of phonemes (*vaṇṇalopa*).
43. By the elision of the vowel *a* in *paṭisaṅkhāya yoniso*, there is the form *paṭisaṅkhāyoniso*.
In cases such as *alābu*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*: "the gourds sink" (*lābu sīdanti*) and "stones float" (*silā plavanti*).
44. A change of letter (*vikāra*) also occurs for the sake of breaking up the meter.
In "akaramhase te" and so forth, by this [rule], the long *e*-vowel in the heavy syllable *sakāre* becomes a short vowel;
thus: "akaramhasa te kiccaṃ. 45. The restriction of syllables constitutes *chanda*; the restriction of heavy and light [syllables] constitutes *vutti*.
A long vowel is heavy, as is a short vowel preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*); however, a short vowel [not so preceded] is light. For example: *ā*, *assa*, *aṃ*, *a*.
In this way, others too should be understood: the *saṃhitā* is beneficial for the *tanti*.
And *saṃhitā* [occurs] through the proximity or intervention of phonemes.
This is the mixed junction (*vomissakasandhi*).
2. Nāmakaṇḍa, Masculine Gender 47.
“Connected with the words of the Jina” is the governing rule for all [subsequent] instances.
And the gender is determined.
A form of speech associated with meaning, excluding roots, suffixes, and case-endings, is called "gender" (liṅga). Here, the gender suitable for the Victor’s word is both established and produced.
When the word "Buddha" stands [as a base]: 48. When "Buddha" is present—

And then there are the case-endings (*vibhattiyo*). Therefore, the case-endings follow the gender-words (*liṅga*). By means of the letter *ca*, their designations as singular, etc., and nominative, etc., are also [established].
The case-endings are: *si, yo, aṃ, yo, nā, hi, sa, naṃ, smā, hi, sa, naṃ, smiṃ, su*. *Si* and *yo* are the nominative (*paṭhamā*).
*Am* (in *yo*) is the second case; *nā hi* (in *nāhi*) is the third case; *sa naṃ* (in *saṃ*) is the fourth case; *smā hi* (in *smāhi*) is the fifth case;
*sa naṃ* (in *saṃ*) is the sixth case; *smiṃ su* (in *su*) is the seventh case.
The first case occurs in the sense of gender (*liṅgatthe*).
That pure meaning of the noun-base (*sadda-rūpa*) which has not yet entered into the internal process of grammatical relations such as agent and object is called the "gender-meaning" (*liṅgattha*);

when there is merely the expression of that [meaning], the first case-ending occurs. Regarding its application, when singularity is to be expressed, the singular number (*ekavacana*) is used. It is called "number" (*vacana*) because it is spoken by means of it;
the expression of a single meaning is "singular number. Likewise for the plural number (*bahuvacana*).
Atotveva.
So. After a word ending in /a/, the following /s/ becomes /o/.
*Saralopo mādesappaccayādimhi*: When there is elision of vowels (*saralopa*) due to a *mādesa* (substitution of *m*), or at the beginning of a suffix, the original form (*pakati*) is restored.

When vowels (*sara*) are followed by *aṃ* and so forth, their elision occurs; once that has been done, if a non-homogeneous vowel (*asavaṇṇa*) is reached by means of *kvacādi*, the original form is restored.
This applies when a subsequent [suffix] is joined. Thus, in the following cases, there is elision of vowels and so on. *Buddho*.
The plural suffix *yo* is used when a plurality is to be expressed.
After this [suffix], there is optionally the substitution of *vā*. For all bases ending in *ā*, the suffix *āe* is used.

After words ending in short *a*, the nominative and accusative case endings (*paṭhamā* and *dutiyā*) optionally become *ā* and *e* respectively. Examples: *buddhā*. Why is it said "optionally" (*vā*)?
[To show that] *agge* [is not an option].
49. In the sense of gender, there is only the nominative (*paṭhamā*).
And in addressing. Addressing (*ālapana*) is the act of making someone face one; when there is a sense of gender exceeding that [mere presence], the nominative case (*paṭhamā*) occurs.
Regarding the rule "In addressing, *si* is designated as *ga*," the designation *ga* applies to *si*. When *ga* is present, it is simply *e*.

The vowel *a* at the end of words such as *pitā* (father) and others becomes *ā* when followed by a consonant (*ge*). When followed by a consonant, the vowel *a* at the end of words such as *pitā*, *satthā*, *attha*, and *rājā* becomes *ā*. Regarding the rule "or *ā*":
when followed by a consonant, the long vowel *ā* may optionally become short.
The *gas* (consonants) are also elided when followed by a *sesa* (remaining suffix).

Those [suffixes] specified as beginning with *si*, *syā*, and *sakhā*, as well as others ending in *avaṇṇa*, *ivaṇṇa*, *uvaṇṇa*, or the letter *o*, are called *sesa*; the *gas* that follow them are elided. Examples: *he* – *buddha*, *buddhā*. *yo* – *buddhā*. 50.
The second case (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the object (*kamma*).
Whatever one performs is called *kamma* (action). In that context, the second case ending occurs [after the word]. *Aṃbuddhaṃ*. [The rule] "of *yo*, [it becomes] *e* before *buddha*" [applies].
51. Only after the third case ending; and [the suffix] *tva* [is used] for the agent (*kattar*).
He who performs [an action] is called the agent (*kattā*). In that context, the third case ending occurs. *Nā*:
after [the stem-final] *a*, *na* becomes *ena*. *Ato nena*: *na* following an *a*-vowel changes to *ena*. For example: *Buddhena*.
Hi.
In the case of *suhī*, *e* is substituted for *svakāra*.
That is, in the word *suhī*, *e* occurs in place of *sva*.

The endings *smā*, *hi*, *smin*, and *naṃ* [are substituted] for the case endings *mhā*, *abhimhi*, and *vā*. After all preceding sounds, the endings *smā*, *hi*, *smin*, and *naṃ* become respectively *mhā*, *abhimhi*, and *vā*. Examples: *buddhebhi*, *buddhehi*. 52.
The third case ending is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
Or, that by which one performs [an action] is called the instrument (*karaṇa*). In that case, the third case ending occurs. It is entirely equal to the agent (*kartṛ*). 53.
The fourth case ending occurs in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*).
That toward whom one wishes to give, or who approves of it, or for whom one maintains [it], is called the recipient. In that case, the fourth case ending occurs. *Sa*.
Therefore, it is indeed so.
For the dative singular, *āyo* [is substituted] for *a*.
After the vowel *a*, the dative singular ending becomes optionally *āyo*. [Example: *Buddhāya*.
“*Sāgamo se*” means that the letter *sa* is inserted after *se*. [This applies to] *buddhassa*,
*naṃ*, *dīghanta eva*,
and *sunaṃhisu*.
In the presence of *su*, *naṃ*, *hi*, and *su* [as suffixes], the long vowel occurs for *sa-ra* and so forth. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is not so in some cases. [Examples: *buddhānaṃ*. 54.
The fifth case is used for the ablative (*apādāna*).
That from which one departs, or from which one takes fear, is called the ablative; in that case, the fifth case is employed. [The suffix is] *smā*.
Therefore, it is thus:
55. *Smā* and *asmim* become *ā* or *e* before other vowels. *Buddhā*, *buddhamhā*, *buddhasmā*; *buddhebhi*, *buddhehi*.
56. The sixth case [is used] for the owner (*sāmī*).
Or, that which is someone’s possession is called "the owner. In that context, the sixth case occurs: *buddhassa* (of the Buddha), *buddhānaṃ* (of the Buddhas).
57. The seventh case [is used] for location (*okāsa*).
Yodhāro, [this is] the section on *tamokāsa*. In that regard, the seventh [case ending] occurs: *smiṃ-buddhe*, *buddhamhi*, *buddhasmiṃ*; [and] *su-buddhesu*.
The Buddha gives happiness to the one who remembers him; what is more difficult than that?
Even sages of great power are born happy through the Buddha.
I shall fix my mind on the Buddhas alone; may I attain the deathless state of the Buddhas.

In those compounds whose meanings are joined, the case endings of the preceding and following members are elided; by the word "and" (ca), in some instances they are not.
Following that, when there is the possibility of a formal derivation such as *mahanta-vīra*—
"And its original form when ending in a vowel.

When the case endings have been elided, the original form (*pakati*) of that compound word—which existed prior [to the elision]—whether it occurred before or after [the elided suffix], becomes [the base]. Thus, the elided vowels are restored.
Then, with "mahanta vīra" standing [as the result]:
In the rule “*mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade*,” *mahā* is the form of *mahanta*.
The suffixes called *taddhita*, compounds (*samāsa*), and *kitaka*, as well as [suffixes] such as *nāman*,
*vāta*, and *vetuna*, should be regarded as nouns (*nāma*), with the exception of the suffixes *tave* and so forth.
From that, there arise [compounds] such as *vatticchā* and *syādi*. Examples include *mahāvīro* and *mahāvīrā*, and so forth.
(204) The *kammadhāraya*, the *dvanda*, and the *tappurisa* possess the gender of the following word (*parapada*);
the *bahubbīhi* possesses the gender of the preceding word (*padantara*).

205. *Rattā* (red) and it is a *paṭī* (garment), thus *rattapaṭī*; *mahantī* (great) and she is *saddhā* (faith), thus *mahāsaddhā*. Here, by the rule "if there is a *kammadhāraya* designation," the preceding member is treated as masculine (*puṃ*), which results in the removal of the feminine suffixes *ā* and *ī*.

206. It is both *nīlaṃ* (blue) and that *uppalaṃ* (lotus), thus *nīluppalaṃ*; *satthī* (thigh) is like *satthi*, and she is both *satthī* and *sāmā* (dark-complexioned), thus *satthisāmā*. The face itself is the moon, thus *mukhacando*.

Because the qualifier and the qualified may appear in either order according to preference—as in *khattiyabhūto* ("one who has become a noble") and so forth—the desired sequence follows the speaker's wish.
Both [types] are *tappurisa* compounds (207).
The word *na* undergoes elision (*lopa*). *Na sura* becomes *asura*.

Here, once the *kammadhāraya* compound has been formed, the designation *tappurisa* applies by the rule “both [types] are *tappurisa*. By the rule “in a *tappurisa*, *na* becomes *a*,” the *na* becomes *a*. *Na asso* becomes *anasso*. Here, by the rule “*ana* [replaces *na*] before a vowel,” the *na* becomes *ana*.
208. Regarding the rule "the compounding of nouns" (*nāmānaṃ samāso*), when the sūtra is split into two parts, there are instances where even words with incompatible meanings may be compounded.

For example: *na puna geyyā apunageyyā gāthā*. Here, the negative particle *na*, which is connected to *geyya*, is compounded with *puna*—despite their incompatible meanings—by virtue of the power of the analytical division (*yogavibhāga*). This is a *digu* compound.
209. When the three worlds (*tayo lokā*) are combined, it becomes *tiloka*.

Here, by the rule "a numeral preceding [a noun] is designated as a *digū*," the compound receives the technical name *digū*, which is a type of *kammadhāraya*. Regarding the rule "a *digū* has singularity," there is both singularity and neuter gender.
This is a pure *tappurisa* compound.
210. *Tappurisa* (Dependent Determinative Compound).
When words beginning with *amā* and others are compounded with subsequent words—namely nouns ending in the accusative case and so forth—that compound is called *tappurisa*.
*Gāmaṃ gato* means "gone to the village.
In the phrase *passa vāsiṭṭha gāmaṃ, gato tisso sāvatthim*, there is no compound because of the presence of the particle *vā*. The same should be understood for other cases.
211. *Raññā hato* means "killed by the king" (*rājahato*).
*Kiccanta* refers to words with a superlative sense (*adhik’atthavacana*).
The suffixes *tabba*, *anīya*, *ṇya*, *teyya*, and *ricca* are *kicca*. A word expressing a superlative sense is one that conveys praise, censure, or an imputed meaning;
for example, *soṇaleyyo kūpo* (“the well licked by the monkey”). Because it is full in such a way that it is licked by monkeys, it is a term of praise.
Because it is leftover from those [others], there is also censure.

"Dadhibhojana" (curd-food) is food moistened with curd; since the act of moistening is expressed by the compound word itself, there is no lack of syntactic connection (*āyuttattha*) here. The application of the word *upasitta* (moistened) has already occurred previously.
212. In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), however: "a quarrel with a sword" is *asinā kalaho*, *asikalaho*.
213. *Buddhassa deyyaṃ* (that which is to be given to the Buddha) is *buddhaddeyyaṃ*; here there is the elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti*).
Likewise for *attanopadaṃ* and so forth. 214. Fear from a thief is *corabhayaṃ*. Likewise for *baddhanamuttaṃ* (the released from the bound) and so forth.
215. The king’s son is *rājaputto*.
In the expression “brāhmaṇassa kaṇhā dantā,” the genitive case is dependent on *dantā* (teeth); because there is no connection with *kaṇha* (black), no compound is formed.
However, when it is a *kammadhāraya* (descriptive) compound—namely, "those which are black and those which are teeth"—then the genitive is dependent on *kaṇhadantā*;
thus, the compound *brāhmaṇakaṇhadantā* certainly occurs.
216. In the expression “rañño māgadhassa dhanaṃ,” the genitive case *rañño* depends on *dhana*, not on *māgadha*.

Since the word *rājā* alone is expressed by the term *māgadha*, there is no distinction [between them] and thus no relationship; therefore, because they share the same referent (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), the word *rājā* is not compounded with *māgadha*.
For a relationship exists between two distinct things.

In the phrase "rañño asso puriso ce" (if there is the king’s horse and the king’s man), because there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekkhatā*) due to each term being connected individually— as "the king’s horse" and "the king’s man"— a compound (*samāsa*) does not occur. However,
when a copulative compound (*dvanda*) is formed as "asso ca puriso ca" (horse and man), the form "rājassapurisā" indeed occurs,
because there is no mutual expectancy between the terms.

In the expression “*rañño garuputto*,” there is a compound (*samāsa*) of *garu* (heavy/respectable) with *putta* (son), even though it depends on *rājā* (king), because it conveys the meaning (*gamakattā*).
The capacity to convey the meaning is indeed the basis for a compound. In that case, the analysis (*viggaha*) is “the son of the respectable one” (*garuno putto*); the same applies elsewhere. 217.
A perception of form is “form-perception” (*rūpasaññā*).

In some cases, this is a term of reproach—such as *kūpamaṇḍūka* ("well-frog"), like a frog in a well; likewise *nagarakāka* ("city-crow") and so forth. Here, reproach is understood through the metaphor.
In compounds such as *antevāsika*, there is an elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti*).
This is a *bahubbīhi* compound.
218. *Aññapadatthesu bahubbīhi*.
When two or more nouns are compounded in the sense of words other than those [already mentioned] ending in the first case (*appaṭhamanta*), that compound is called *bahubbīhi*.
For example: "The monastery to which monks have come" is *āgatasamaṇo vihāro*.

219. He by whom the sense-faculties (*indriya*) have been conquered is "one who has conquered the faculties" (*jitindriya*), namely the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). He by whom the fire has been established is "one who has established the fire" (*āhitaggi*). Or, as in *agyāhita* and other such cases, the qualifying term may optionally follow [the qualified]. 220.
But in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), he by whom a tree has been cut is "one who has cut a tree" (*chinnarukkha*), namely the axe (*pharasu*).
221. He to whom a tax has been given is "one to whom tax has been given" (*dinnasuṅka*), namely the king (*rājā*).
222. Because people have departed from it, it is a *niggatajana* (a village from which people have departed).

223. He who possesses the ten powers is the *dasabala*, the Blessed One. He who has no equal is the *asama*. Here, by means of the analysis of grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*), there is the elision of *na* [to form] *a* in the word *attanna*.

He whose tongue is abundant is the *pahūtajivha*; he whose wisdom is great is the *mahāpañña*. In the two instances [of *pahūta-* and *mahā-*], because of the extension of the masculine state according to the rule "in the case of feminine bases, the masculine state applies when followed by a feminine or masculine [word]," there is the absence of the *āī* suffixes in the preceding and following members.
224. “In some cases, the final *a* of those ending in a compound [is elided]. Here, *anta* refers to the end of the word. By the inclusion of the term *kāra*, both *ā* and *i* are also included.
Feminine bases ending in *ī* and *u*, as well as those ending in *tv*, also undergo the *ka* suffix. For example: one whose eye (*akkhi*) is broad (*visāla*) is *visālakkha*;

*paccakkhadhammā* (where there is elision of the suffix). One whose fragrance (*gandha*) is beautiful (*sobhana*) is *sugandhi*. *Bahukantika* (having many desires), *bahunadika* (having many rivers), *samuddo* (the ocean). In this context...
The short vowel [is substituted] by *yadādinā*. *Bahukattuko*: that forest in which there are many intoxicated elephants (*mātaṅga*) is "possessing many intoxicated elephants" (*mattabahumātaṅga*);

this is a coordinate compound (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). 225. That which has a color like gold is "gold-colored" (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇo*). He who has a thunderbolt (*vajira*) in his hand is "thunderbolt-handed" (*vajirapāṇi*). He who has hair on his chest is "chest-haired" (*urasilomo*); here there is the elision of the case-ending (*vibhattialopa*).
“Atthesu”: by taking this in the sense of plurality, it refers even to some nominative singular forms. That which exists together with a cause is "sahetuka" (with-cause);

that which is accompanied by "yadā" and so forth is "sahassa" (with). "Satta vā aṭṭha vā" means seven or eight; "māsā" (months) is here either the external referent (*aññapadattha*) or the meaning of the word itself. That which is the intermediate space between the southern and eastern directions is "dakkhiṇapubbā," the direction. This is a case of different grammatical bases (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*).
Regarding "those who do not go first": what is it? It is the Dhamma which was taught by the Buddha.
227. *Dvandva* compound:
A collection of nouns is a *dvandva*.
"Collection" (*samuccaya*) means a grouping together. That collection of nouns which share the same case-ending is called a *dvanda* compound; this rule concerns the plural number. For example:

"the moon and the sun" (*candasūriyā*). In such cases as "they stand," etc., because of the commonality of their connection to the action, there is here a single meaning (*apekatthatā*); likewise for "men and women" (*naranāriyo*), and for syllables and words.

228. Likewise, in a *dvanda* compound, there is singularity and neuter gender for parts of the body, musical instruments, vehicles, army divisions, small creatures, various things that are opposed (*vividhaviruddha*), dissimilar things (*visabhāga*), and so forth.

"Various and opposed" means *vividhaviruddha*; "dissimilar" (*visabhāga*) refers to those things that are both various and similar (*sabhāga*). Just as in a *digu* compound, so too in a *dvanda*, there is singularity and neuter gender for parts of the body and the like.

Examples: eye and ear (*cakkhusotaṃ*); song and instrumental music (*gītavāditaṃ*); yoke and plough (*yuganaṅgalaṃ*); sword and shield (*asicammaṃ*); gadfly and mosquito (*ḍaṃsamakasaṃ*); crow and owl (*kokālūkaṃ*).

Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): name has the characteristic of bending (*namana*), and form has the characteristic of being affected (*ruppana*). Thus these phenomena are diverse according to their characteristics, yet they are similar from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other instances are also included. For example: [the compound] of words with different genders—*itthipumaṃ*; by means of *ya* and so forth, the short vowel occurs—as in *dāsidāsaṃ* (female and male slave) and *pattacīvaraṃ* (bowl and robe); [the compound] *gaṅgāsoṇaṃ* (the Ganges and the Soṇa river).
[The compound] of numbers and measures—as in *tikacatukkaṃ* (a triad and a tetrad).
Among artisans, the bamboo-worker and chariot-maker;
among hunters, the fowler and deer-trapper;
among those of low birth, the iron-smith.
For Brahmins who study a single recension—such as the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas (etc.).
229. There is optionally a singular number and neuter gender for trees, grass, cattle, wealth, grain, countries, and so forth, when they appear in a dvanda compound.
Dhavakhadiraṃ, dhavakhadirā; muñjapabbajaṃ, muñjapabbajā; ajeḷakaṃ, ajeḷakā; hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ, hiraññasuvaṇṇāni; sāliyavaṃ, sāliyavā;
kāsikosalaṃ, kāsikosalā. By the word "etc.
(ādi), it includes others as well. For example: among things that are eternally opposed and incompatible—kusalākusalaṃ, kusalākusalāni.
Of birds: *bakabalākaṃ*, *bakabalākā*.
Of words: *dadhighataṃ*, *dadhighatāni*.
Of directions: *pubbāparaṃ*, *pubbāparā*, and so forth.
Abyayībhāva compound (230):

The word *adhi* [is used] in the sense of the locative (*smiṃ*), and its [locative ending] is elided. Because it shares the same grammatical base (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) with the word *itthi*, it also applies to the word *itthiyam*. Since it is a compulsory compound (*niccasamāsa*), the analysis is performed by means of another phrase: "this woman who serves as the locus" (*ādhārabhūtāyamitthiyam*).
When *adhi-itthiyam* stands thus—being preceded by a prefix (*upasagga*) or a particle (*nipāta*)—it is an *abyayībhāva*.
A word preceded by a prefix (*upasagga*) and so forth forms a compound in the sense of a case ending and the like, and it is designated as an *abyayībhāva*.
"It is neuter" means that the *abyayībhāva* is neuter; by [the rule] beginning with *yadādi*, it takes the singular number.
By [the rule] "a vowel is short in the neuter," the vowel is shortened.

"And there is elision [of the case ending] after another [type of compound]. All case endings following an *abyayībhāva* compound that ends in the vowel *a* are elided. *Adhitthi*: the meaning of the case endings is "locus" (*ādhāra*) and so forth.
Here, the word *adhi* functions in the sense of a locus; this word *adhitthi* expresses the meaning "in the feminine."

*Samīpaṃ* means near the city; *upanagaraṃ* (near the city). Regarding the rule *“aṃ vibhattīnam akārantabyayībhāvā”* (the suffix *aṃ* is substituted for case endings in neuter indeclinable compounds ending in *a*), the word *kvaci* (sometimes) is used. Why [is it] *kvaci*? [To show that it does not apply in other cases, as in: *upanagare* (in the vicinity of the city).

*Abhāvo* (absence) [as in] *nimmakkhikaṃ* (free from flies), where the vowel is shortened. *Anu* prefixed [to *thera*] gives *anutheraṃ* (junior elder); *yathāsattiṃ* (according to power), meaning not exceeding one's power.
"Ye ye buddhā yathābuddhaṃ" means according to their respective ages.
"Yattako paricchedo jīvassa yāvajīvaṃ" means for as long as the limit of life lasts; it is used in the sense of restriction.

"Ā pabbatā khettaṃ āpabbataṃ khettaṃ" means a field up to the mountain; it denotes a boundary. A boundary (sīmā) that is being traversed is a limit (mariyādā); the meaning is a boundary excluding the mountain.
“Ā jalantā sītaṃ ājalantaṃ sītaṃ”: here *ā* signifies inclusion (*abhividhi*). When the boundary (*sīmā*) is being grasped as inclusive, it means "together with that which is burning.
Due to the connection with the word *ā*, the sentence is established by the rule for the ablative case beginning with "dhātunāmā" and so forth. It is the same elsewhere.
However, in cases such as “Uttamo vīro pavīro,” there is no *abyayībhāva* compound because the meaning of the preceding member (*pubbapadattha*) is not predominant.
It is only a *kammadhāraya* compound. Thus, the Dhamma that is distinguished (*visiṭṭha*) is the Abhidhamma. Bad food is *kadanna*;
here, by the rule *“kada kussā”* [Kacc 325], there is the substitution of *kada* for *kusa* before a vowel.

Little salt is *kālavaṇa*; here, by the rule *“kāppatthesu ca”* [Kacc 326], there is the substitution of *kā* for *kusa*, and by the use of the plural, this occurs elsewhere as well. A contemptible man is a *kāpurisa* or a *kupurisa*; likewise with *asura* and so forth.
The *abyayībhāva* compound is that in which the meaning of another word is predominant, whether it precedes, follows, or stands between [the members].
The *kammadhāraya*, *tappurisa*, *dvanda*, and *bahubbīhi* are to be known as the [remaining] compounds. Thus ends the section on compounds (*samāsa*).
4. The Section on Secondary Derivatives (Taddhitakaṇḍa): Secondary Derivatives Not Ending in -t (Apaccataddhita) 232.
[The suffix] -vāna occurs after the word *paca*.

After words ending in the sixth case, the suffix *ṇo* optionally occurs in the sense of "belonging to that" (*tassāpacca*). The word *vā* indicates that it is optional. Since the meaning of "belonging to that" is already expressed by *ṇo* itself, the word *apacca* is not employed.
By the phrase "of those, [there is] elision of the case-ending," the case-ending is elided through the mention of "those. The same applies further on.
By the rule "of those, there is elision of *ṇa*," there is the elision of the *ṇa* of the suffixes.

“Or, for a vowel with an initial *ā* sound, or for one at the end of a conjunct, there is *vṛddhi* if followed by *saṇ*”: when the letter *saṇ* follows, there is *vṛddhi* for a vowel with an initial *ā* sound that is not at the end of a conjunct.
Regarding its restriction:
“And for vowels *a* and *u*, *āy* is the *vṛddhi*.”
The *ā* and *ē* vowel increments occur for the vowels *a* and *ā*, though not in some instances due to the word *ca*.
Following the elision of the *sara* (vowels) and so forth, the case endings (*syādi*) are applied as if it were a noun (*nāma*), because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
The gender, case ending, and number should correspond to those expressed by the secondary derivative.

The suffix *ṇya* occurs after a collective noun (*samūhabhāva*) in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*), and it is neuter. Those [suffixes] ending in *tuttha* are indeclinables (*nipāta*). The suffixes *dhā*, *mi*, *thaṃ*, and *paccaya* are also included.

A person who is a descendant (*apacca*) of Vasiṭṭha is *vāsiṭṭha*; a woman is *vāsiṭṭhī*; and the neuter is *vāsiṭṭhaṃ*. Because of the rule allowing for an option (*vikappavidhāna*), and because the formation with the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) supersedes the formation with a compound (*samāsa*), there is also the form *vasiṭṭhā* as a descendant.
"Or by a neuter [word]," so the wise who are learned in the science of grammar know.
(233) "Vā" and "apacca" are the governing rules (*adhikāra*).
"Ṇāyana," "Ṇāna," and "vaccha" follow from this point onward.
From the clan-group beginning with Vaccha, the suffixes *ṇāyana* or *ṇa* are used for the name.

A descendant from the great-grandson onwards is a *gotta* (clan). The descendant of Kacca is Kaccāyana or Kaccāna; because it ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoganta*), there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*).
234. According to the rule “*ṇeyyo* [is used] after Kattiya and others,” the suffix *ṇeyya* is applied: the descendant of Vinatā is Venateyya or Vinateyya. Not in the alternative view.

By means of a split in the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*), [the suffix] *ṇeya* is applied even in the sense of "that to which something is given" (*tassa dīyate*); thus, one to whom a sacrificial fee (*dakkhiṇā*) is given is a "recipient of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*).

235. *Ato ṇi vā*: After a word ending in the letter *a*, the suffix *ṇi* optionally occurs when it does not denote a descendant (*apacca*). By the repetition of the word "optionally" (*vā*), the suffix *ṇika* is also included; furthermore, after words ending in *a* as well as those not ending in *a*, the suffix *ba* also occurs.
*Dakkhi*, *sakyaputtika*, *maṇḍabba*, *bhātubba*. [The suffix] *dvitta* is added. 236.
By the rule "Ṇava after *pagu* and so forth," the suffix *Ṇava* is applied. The descendant of *manu* is *māṇava*. 237.
By the rule "Ṇera after *vidhavā* and so forth," the suffix *Ṇera* is applied; thus, *sāmaṇera*.
238. The secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix *ṇika* has various meanings such as "associated with" (*saṃsaṭṭha*), etc.:
"By means of which one is associated, crosses over, moves about, or carries—[the suffix] *ṇika* [is applied]. By the word "or" (*vā*), there are also multiple meanings and multiple suffixes.

One who is associated with a pot (*ghata*) is a *ghātiko*, [meaning] rice (*odana*). One who crosses over by means of a raft (*uḷūpa*) is an *oḷūpiko* or an *uḷūpiko*; there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) in the alternative form.
One who travels by cart is a *sākaṭika*. One who carries on the head is a *sīsika*;

there is no vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*). From the feminine gender, the suffixes *-eyyaka* and *-ṇaka* are applied. One born in Campā is a *campēyyaka*; likewise, one from Bārāṇasī is a *bārāṇaseyyaka*.
With the suffix *-ṇaka*: one who dwells in Kusinārā is a *kosināraka*. From the name of a country, the suffix *-ṇaka* is also used: one who dwells in Magadha, or the lord of them, is a *māgadhaka*.

*Ājānīya*: one who is distinguished among those of that same class; a horse distinguished among the breed of horses is an *assājānīya*. *Ño*: "to be known as the foremost" (*aggañña*)—this is a double suffix (*dvitta*). 239.

[The suffix] *ṇika* occurs after the word *tad* in the senses of "studying that," "made by that," and so forth, as well as in the senses of "provision," "application," "craft," "merchandise," and "livelihood.

In phrases such as "he studies that" (*tam adhīte*), the suffix *ṇika* optionally occurs after *tad* and others, with the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including words like *hatādi*. For example: *abhidhammam adhīte* ("he studies the Abhidhamma").
*Ābhidhammiko* or *abhidhammiko*: there is no increase (*vuddhi*) in the suffix. That which is done by speech is *vācasika*. Likewise for *mānasika*.
Here, by the recurrence of the word *ādi* from the rule "there is the addition of *sa* after a vowel" (*sa sare vāgamo*), there is the addition of *sa*.

Because it is located in the body, feeling is *sārīrikā*. One who is appointed at a gate is a *dovāriko*; here, by the rule "the addition of *o* occurs in place of *māyūna*," there is the addition of the letter *o* before the letter *va*.
*Sippa* means arts such as singing and so forth. One whose craft (*sippa*) is the lute (*vīṇā*) is a *veṇika*; here, "lute" refers to the playing of the lute.
One whose merchandise (*bhaṇḍa*) is perfume (*gandha*) is a *gandhika*. One who lives by killing deer (*maga*) is a *māgavika*; there is the insertion of the letter *va*.

One killed with a net is a *jālika*; one bound with a thread is a *suttika*. One whose weapon (*āyudha*) is a bow (*cāpa*) is a *cāpika*. Or, one who has wind (*vāta*) as his affliction (*ābādha*) is a *vātika*.
One who has faith in the Buddha is a *buddhika*; a commodity purchased with cloth is *vatthika*.

That which has a *kumbha* (a jar) as its measure is *kumbhika*; or a heap of those [commodities] is also *kumbhika*. One who plays with dice is *akkhika*; one who dwells in Magadha or is born there is *māgadhika*, and so forth. 240.
The suffix *-ṇa* [is used after words such as] *rāga* in the sense of "colored by that," and in other senses as well.
The suffix *ṇo* optionally occurs after the word *ratta* (red) and in other such senses. *Kasāvena rattaṃ* becomes *kāsāvaṃ* (ochre).
Likewise, *nīlaṃ*, *pītaṃ*, and so forth. There is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). *Mahisassa idaṃ* becomes *māhisaṃ* (belonging to a buffalo), [referring to] a horn.
Similarly, *rājaporisaṃ*. Here, by the rule "of *a* and *yu* vowels" and by the subsequent mention of "strengthening," there is strengthening of the second member of the compound.
*Māgadha* means one who has come from Magadha, was born there, is the lord of them, or for whom they are the residence;
*kattika* is the month associated with the month of Kattika and so forth;

*buddha* is one whose deity is the Buddha; *veyyākaraṇa* is one who has studied grammar (*byākaraṇa*) after having understood it; here, by the rule "māyūnamā" etc., the augment *e* is inserted before the letter *y*, and that *y* undergoes doubling (*dvitta*); *sāgara* is that which is produced from the *sagara*s (oceans), and so on.

241. *Jātādīnam imiyā ca*: In the case of words such as *jāta*, the suffixes *-imiya* and *-iya* occur; by the word *ca* ("and"), *-kiya* is also included. That which is born later is *pacchima*; one born of the human species (*manussa-jāti*) is *manussajātiya*. That which is fixed at the end is *antima*; [the feminine form is] *antiya*.
Likewise, *andhakiya*. One who has a son is *puttima*; [the feminine form is] *puttiya*. Likewise, *kappiya*.
242. “*Tadassaṭṭhānamīyo ce*” means *īyo*. By the letter *ca*, it is also used in the sense of “suitable for” (*hita*) and so forth. A place for binding is *bandhanīya*;
what is suitable for walking is *caṅkamanīya*. 243. “*Ālu tabbahule*” means *ālu*. One who has much covetousness is *abhijjhālu*. This is a particular type of secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
244. *Visese taratamissikiyiṭṭhā*:
the suffixes *tara*, etc., occur in the sense of excellence (*atisaya*).
"This one is more wicked than these" is expressed as *pāpataro*, *pāpatamo*, *pāpissiko*, *pāpiyo*, or *pāpiṭṭho*.

In the rule “*vuddhassa jo iṭṭhesu*,” for the substitution of *ja* in place of *vuddha*—due to the elision of the *sar* [prefix] and so forth by the inclusion of the base form (*pakati*)—the *i* of *issa* [is elided].
Thus: *jeyya*, *jeṭṭha*. Likewise, in the rule “*pasatthassa so ce*,” for the substitution of *sa*—[there is] *seyya*, *seṭṭha*. [This applies when] a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *a* follows.
245. “*Tadassatthīti vī*” means *vī*. When one possesses wisdom (*medhā*), one is called *medhāvī*.
246. Likewise, “*tapādito sī*” means *sī*, with double-consonant doubling (*dvitta*);
thus, *tapassī*. 247. “*Daṇḍādito ika ī*” means *ika* and *ī*. Thus, *daṇḍika* and *daṇḍī*.
248. “From *guṇa* and so forth, *vantu*” means *vantu*. [Examples: *guṇavā*, *paññavā*. By the rule beginning with *yadādi*, the vowel is shortened.
249. “From *sati* and so forth, *mantu*” means *mantu*. [Examples: *satimā*, *bhānumā*. 250.
“In *āyu*, *su*, *kāra*, and *asman*, *mhu* becomes *ssa*. [Example: *āyasmā*.
251. By the rule “*saddhādito ṇa*,” the suffix *ṇa* is applied. Thus: *saddho*. 252.

By the rule “*tappakativacane mayo*,” the suffix *maya* is applied. Thus: *sovaṇṇamayaṃ*, meaning "made of gold" (*suvaṇṇena pakataṃ*), or simply "gold. In the alternative view, there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) by the rule beginning with "*yadādi*," and then the elision of these [suffixes].
When the vibhatti suffix is elided, the final letter of *mano* and other such words becomes *o*. *Manomayaṃ*.
[Rule 253] *Saṅkhyātaddhita*:
The section concerning the suffix *tya* for completing a number begins.
“From *dvi* and *ti*, *tīya*; from *ti*, *du* as well”: thus, the *du* of *dvi*. That which completes two is *dvitīya*; likewise, *tṛtīya*. 254.
“From *catur* and *ṣaṣ*, *tha* and *ṭha*”: thus, *caturtha* and *ṣaṣṭha*. 255.
With the prefix *addha* (half) applied to these, there are *addhuḍḍha*, *divaḍḍha*, *diyaḍḍha*, and *addhatiya*.
When combined with the half-unit (*aḍḍha*) as a secondary member (*upapada*), the fourth, second, and third become *aḍḍhuḍḍha*, *divaḍḍha*, and *diyaḍḍhāḍḍhatiya*.
The fourth by means of a half is *aḍḍhuḍḍha*; the second by means of a half is *divaḍḍha* or *diyaḍḍha*; the third by means of a half is *aḍḍhatiya*. 256.
By the rule “*mo* [is the suffix] for completing a number,” *mo* is added; thus, the fifth (*pañcamo*). In the feminine, that which completes five is *pañcamī*.
When "eka" and "dasa" are formed into a *dvanda* compound—meaning "one and ten"—the vowel *ā* optionally replaces the final syllable of these two words.

When a numeral is the final member of a compound, the vowel *ā* optionally replaces the final syllable of "dvi," "eka," and "aṭṭha. Thus: *ekādasa* (or *ekādasā*) means "eleven"; likewise, *dvādasa* (or *dvādasā*) means "twelve."

When *tissa* is substituted for *te* by the rule beginning with *yadādinā*, then by the rule *“ekādito dassa ra saṅkhyāne”* (in counting, *da* becomes *ra* after *eka* and so on), the *da* in the word *dasa* becomes *ra*. Thus: *terasa*. 257.

By the rule *“catūpapadassa lopo tuttarapadādicassa cucopi navā”* (there is elision of the *tu* of the word *catus*, and optionally the *ca* of the initial of the following word), there is elision of the *tu* in the word *catus* and its replacement by *cu*. Thus: *cuddasa*.

By the rule *“dase so niccañce”* (after *dasa*, *cha* is always replaced by *so*), there is the substitution of *so* for *cha*. Then, by the rule *“ḷa darānaṃ”* (for *da* and *ra*, there is *ḷa*), the *da* in the word *dasa* becomes *ḷa*. Thus: *soḷasa*, *aṭṭhārasa*.
258. Regarding the rule “*vīsati dasesu bā dvissa tū*,” the substitution *bā* occurs for *dvi*. Thus: *bāvīsati* (twenty-two). The eleventh is that which completes the eleven. 259.
Regarding the rule “*ekādito dasassī*,” the suffix *ī* is applied in the feminine. Thus: *ekādasī*, and so forth.
Regarding the rule “*dvādito konekatthe ce*,” the suffix *ka* is applied; thus: *dvikaṃ* (that which has two as its measure). In the same way, *tikaṃ* (three), and so on.
260. “*Samūhatthe kaṇṇā*” means *kaṇ* and *ṇo*. A collection (*samūha*) of humans is *mānussaka*, or *mānussa*.

When *ṇa* is applied—by the rule “*Jhalānam iyuvā sare vā*,” with the alternative option (*vā*), there is the substitution of *ay* for *iss*—there are two forms: *dvayaṃ* and *tayaṃ*. Similarly, [from the rule] “*Gāmajanabandhusahāyādīhi tā*,” there is *tā*: *gāmatā*, *nāgaratā*. These are *taddhita* suffixes expressing the state (*bhāva*).
261. The suffixes *ṇya* and *tta* occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).

In the sense of the abstract state, *ṇya* and *tta* occur; by the inclusion of the word "also" (*tu*), *tta* occurs as well. *Ṇya* occurs in the sense of possession (*sakattha*) and so forth, and *tta* occurs in the sense of possession.
From these, words and knowledge arise.
Being (bhāva) is the mode of verbal expression (saddavutti);
name (nāma), which serves as the signifier,
consists of genus (jāti), substance (davba), action (kriyā), and quality (guṇa).

263. For example: the state of the moon is "moon-ness" (*candatta*). Here, by virtue of its name, the word "moon" refers to the physical object (the moon-substance), as does the cognition that conforms to the form of that sign.
Likewise, "human-ness" (*manussatta*) is [determined] by virtue of the human species.

Through the elision of the suffix *i* (from *ādika*), we have "staff-ness" (*daṇḍitta*), which arises from the connection with the staff-substance; "cook-ness" (*pācakatta*), from the connection with the act of cooking; and "blue-ness" (*nīlatta*), by virtue of the quality of blue.
In this way, it should be understood accordingly for the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* as well.

Regarding *ṇya*: "The vowel *a* [at the end of a root] is elided before *ye*, and by the word 'and' (*ca*), the vowel *i* is also [elided]. When *ye* follows, the vowel *a* is elided; by the word 'and' (*ca*), the vowel *i* is also elided.

"In as many consonants as there are, the *cala* (consonant) [is] the quality of being *ja*": thus, for those [consonants] such as *ta* that are joined with the letter *ya*, the letters beginning with *ca* [are substituted].
By the mention of the letter *ka*, in certain cases, the preceding [vowel] together with the following *ya* undergoes the *pubbarūpa* (single-substitute) sandhi, and there is doubling (*dvitta*).
Examples: *paṇḍiccaṃ*, *kosallaṃ*, *sāmaññaṃ*, *sohajjaṃ*, *porissaṃ*, *nepakkaṃ*, *sāruppaṃ*, *osabbhaṃ*, *opammaṃ*.
And *āttañca*.
In these cases, *ā* becomes *ī*, with the insertion of the letter *r* in its place.
By the rule of elision of *sara* (vowels) and so forth, there is the elision of *i*. [The word] *isino* means "the state of being an *isi*."
I shall explain. Thus, *mudutā* (gentleness), *arahatā* (worthiness);

[in] *antassa*, there is elision by means of *yadādi*. *Puthujjanattaṃ* (the state of being a worldling); *akiñcanaṃ* itself is *ākiñcaññaṃ* (nothingness); *kuṇḍaniyā* offspring is *koṇḍañño*; here, by the rule beginning with *vuddhādo*, there is *vuddhi* (vṛddhi) even for that which ends in a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).

*Padāya* beneficial is *pajjaṃ* (footwear); *dhanāyaṃ* conducive is *dhaññaṃ* (grain); *satito* arisen is *saccaṃ* (truth); there is elision of *i*, and there is no *vuddhi* in the three cases. *Devo* itself is *devatā* (a deity).

264. In the phrase “ṇa visamādīhi,” the suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus, *vesamaṃ*. From *ujju*, the abstract state is *ajjavaṃ*. Here, when *ussa* is replaced by *ātte*, the letter *rū* becomes *avo* according to the rule beginning with “yadādi.

265. After words such as *ramaṇīya*, the suffixes *kaṇ* and *ti* are applied. [The suffix] *kaṇ* is added. This applies to all other [words] except for those ending in *māna*. [This is an] indeclinable (*abyaya*) secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

266. Regarding the rule “*vibhāge dhā ce*”: *dhā* is used; by the letter *ca*, the suffix *soppa* is also included. By one division (*vibhāga*), it is “in one way” (*ekadhā*); due to its being a particle (*nipāta*), there is elision of the final vowel. By division of words (*padavibhāga*), it is “word by word” (*padaso*). 267. Regarding the rule “*sabbanāmehi pakāravacane tu thā*”:
*thā* is used; by the letter *tu*, the form *thattha* is also included. Every manner (*pakāra*), or by every manner, is “in every way” (*sabbathā*).

Likewise for “in another way” (*aññathā*). 268. Regarding the rule “*kimimehi thaṃ*”: *thaṃ* is used. With the substitution of *ka*, it becomes “how? (*kathaṃ*). With the substitution of *i*, it becomes “thus” (*itthaṃ*). By the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), *thaṃ* is used for the plural: “in many ways” (*bahutthaṃ*).

269. When the sense of "making something that is not so, to be so" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is implied, the suffix *ī* is added after a noun when it is joined with the verb *karoti*, provided it begins with a vowel;
for example, *malinīkaroti setaṃ* ("he makes the white thing dirty"). "The making of what was not ash into ash" is *bhasmīkaraṇaṃ kaṭṭhassa* ("the reducing of wood to ashes").
"That which was not dirty becomes dirty" is *malinībhavati seto*. The suffix *ī* is also a particle (*nipāta*). [This applies] when there is the state of becoming what one was not previously.
What is meant by "in connection with *kar* and *bhū*"? For example: *ghaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a pot), *ghaṭo bhavati* (it becomes a pot).
Why is it said "in connection with *kar* and *bhū*"? Consider: *amalino malino jāyate* (the unstained becomes stained).
[The rule applies] when there is a change of state (*avasthāntara*) in the entity (*vastu*) that is already existent (*bhūta*).
The becoming of that state is known by the wise as *abhūtatadbhāva*. [This is] a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
